note: A blocker is a dated claim, not a property of the world. The practitioner's rule of 2026-10-12: even blockers are not permanent, and each should be revisited in DE mode. This file exists because the two blockers recorded in TODO.md went unexamined and both were wrong when finally re-derived on the day this file was written -- one had been lifted by a widget that shipped, and the other was half true and had been stopping work it did not actually block. A blocker nobody re-derives does the same damage as an admission nobody re-reviews: it looks like a fact and acts like a decision. Every entry must therefore carry a liftTest -- the check that would show it has gone -- because a blocker with no stated lift test cannot be falsified and is only a mood. The ratchet is the revisit window: scripts/validate-blockers.mjs fails when a standing blocker has not been revisited within it.
windowBasis: This project adds and retires widgets in days, not months: twelve widgets arrived in three days and three were retired in one. A blocker older than a week has outlived the conditions it was recorded under.

blockers.liftTest: A declared field schema exists for table, raster and network inputs, with per-field type and unit, and a role binding can be offered against it.
blockers.whatChanged: The claim was true and its scope was not. It was recorded as blocking the ruleset widget outright, and it does block the general form -- binding any field of any input to a declared role. It does not block the merge that reduces the widget count, because the three existing fact generators take typed carriers and not arbitrary attribute tables: makeN3(NearestRow[]), accessN3(AccessRow[]), facilityN3(Facility[]). So one widget can host the three rulesets as declared data with their existing fact generation, which is 4 widgets to 1, while generic binding waits for the schema. A blocker stated one size too large had been stopping work it did not block.

blockers.claim: No widget takes an area and a point layer and outputs the points inside it. coverage_check does the geometry and emits a review carrier consumed only by map_output and table_output, so a spatial selection cannot be chained into anything.
blockers.liftTest: A primitive takes (area, points) and outputs points, and the Old Naledi example produces its facility set from buffer_area plus that selection, with the difference from the shipped selection stated rather than discovered.
blockers.measured: Measured across buffer distances 2026-10-12, after the cap was raised. Shipped: a 6 km circle at the boundary's bounding-box centre selects 122 of 214 facilities. Boundary widened by 4,000 m: 93, all of them inside the shipped set. 4,500 m: 109, all inside. 5,000 m: 122, agreeing on 121 with one differing each way. 5,500 m: 139, containing all 122 and 17 more. 6,000 m: 150, containing all 122 and 28 more. So the closest equivalent to the shipped selection is a 5,000 m margin around the boundary, which is a 1-in-122 difference, and that value was inside the old cap all along.
blockers.alsoFound: The 5,000 m cap on validateBuffer was an unjustified knob range -- the geometry helpers in the same module accept 50,000, and validateBufferPointNode delegates to the same function, so one number governed both buffer widgets. Raised to 50,000 on the practitioner's point that it is a knob. It was NOT blocking this replacement, which is a claim recorded an hour earlier and withdrawn by the measurement: 6,000 m over-selects by 28 facilities and 5,000 m is the best match, so the cap never stood in the way.
blockers.narrowedTo: Replaces `facilities-carrier`, recorded an hour earlier, which framed this as a producer-named stud question. It is not: the carrier is downstream of the real gap, which is that the selection has nowhere to come from.

design.question: The practitioner, 2026-10-12: spatial selection potentially has types of outputs -- boolean (all points belong or not), points (which belong, which do not).
design.answer: Those are three LAYERS, not three variants of one widget, and coverage_check already contains all three fused together.
layers: 1 - relation per point. Geometry only, no policy. coverage_check computes SpatialRelation = Inside | Boundary | Outside | MissingLocation, and maps each to GeoSPARQL: sfWithin, sfTouches, sfDisjoint. This is the primitive.
2 - decision per point. A ruleset over the relation. coverage_check has six N3 rules in a template literal concluding fw:coverageDecision over Accept | Review | Excluded.
3 - set-level boolean and counts. An aggregate over the decision. canProceed is three conditions over two counts: rows.length>0 && reviewCount===0 && rows.length>excludedCount.
4 - the filter: relation or decision to points. This is the only genuinely missing piece, and it is what facilities needs.
design.whyNotABooleanPerPoint: It would destroy MissingLocation. A point with no coordinates is not outside; it is unknown, and this project's standing rule is that absence is not a negative. The four-valued relation is how that is kept, and a boolean cannot carry it.
design.whyNotABooleanOutput: 'All points belong' is not a predicate over the relation -- it is a policy applied to it. coverage_check's own rules say so in a comment: 'Boundary points are included by policy.' So the boolean belongs downstream of a ruleset, not as an output mode of a geometry widget. Giving a selection widget output modes would fuse policy back into geometry, which is exactly what coverage_check did.
design.alsoFound: coverage_check's retainedData filters on `excluded`, NOT on relation, so the points it retains INCLUDE Outside ones. It is not the inside-set selection facilities needs, which I had half-assumed it was.

blockers.claim: coverage_check carries six N3 rules as a template literal in src/spatial-coverage.ts, concluding fw:coverageDecision over Accept, Review and Excluded. It is a fourth rule application, and the ruleset ledger records three.
blockers.liftTest: The rules are a declared ruleset in rulesets/ with a basis, an output vocabulary including an unknown value, and byte-identical assembled text, and coverage_check resolves it rather than carrying it.
blockers.whyItMatters: Its policy is stated in a code comment -- 'Boundary points are included by policy' -- and two of its rules map DIFFERENT relations to the SAME decision: Outside to Review and MissingLocation to Review. So the policy collapses outside-ness and unknown-ness, which is the distinction the four-valued relation upstream exists to preserve. Declaring the ruleset makes that choice visible and contestable; a template literal does not. It is also the second OR compiled by hand -- Inside and Boundary both conclude Accept -- after facilityN3's last two rules.
blockers.formExtension: One rule concludes about the ACTIVITY rather than a subject: '{ ?activity fw:checkedRecord ?r. ?r fw:coverageDecision fw:Review. } => { ?activity fw:requiresReview true. }'. Experiment 106's authored form concludes per subject only, so hosting this ruleset needs set-level conclusions, which is a real extension and not a detail.
